{{Short description|Generalisation of the generalised hypergeometric function pFq(z)}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Fox–Wright function''' (also known as '''Fox–Wright Psi function''', not to be confused with [[Wright Omega function]]) is a generalisation of the [[Generalized hypergeometric function|generalised hypergeometric function]] <sub>''p''</sub>''F''<sub>''q''</sub>(''z'') based on ideas of {{harvs|txt|authorlink=Charles Fox (mathematician)|first=Charles|last=Fox|year=1928}} and {{harvs|txt|authorlink=E.M. Wright|first=E. Maitland|last=Wright|year=1935}}:

<math display="block">{}_p\Psi_q \left[\begin{matrix}
( a_1 , A_1 ) & ( a_2 , A_2 ) & \ldots & ( a_p , A_p ) \\
( b_1 , B_1 ) & ( b_2 , B_2 ) & \ldots & ( b_q , B_q ) \end{matrix}
; z \right]
=
\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{\Gamma( a_1 + A_1 n )\cdots\Gamma( a_p + A_p n )}{\Gamma( b_1 + B_1 n )\cdots\Gamma( b_q + B_q n )} \, \frac {z^n} {n!}.
</math>

Upon changing the normalisation

<math display="block">{}_p\Psi^*_q \left[\begin{matrix}
( a_1 , A_1 ) & ( a_2 , A_2 ) & \ldots & ( a_p , A_p ) \\
( b_1 , B_1 ) & ( b_2 , B_2 ) & \ldots & ( b_q , B_q ) \end{matrix}
; z \right]
=
\frac{ \Gamma(b_1) \cdots \Gamma(b_q) }{ \Gamma(a_1) \cdots \Gamma(a_p) }
\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{\Gamma( a_1 + A_1 n )\cdots\Gamma( a_p + A_p n )}{\Gamma( b_1 + B_1 n )\cdots\Gamma( b_q + B_q n )} \, \frac {z^n} {n!}
</math>

it becomes <sub>''p''</sub>''F''<sub>''q''</sub>(''z'') for ''A''<sub>1...''p''</sub> = ''B''<sub>1...''q''</sub> = 1.

The Fox–Wright function is a special case of the [[Fox H-function]] {{harv|Srivastava|Manocha|1984|p=50}}:

<math display="block">{}_p\Psi_q \left[\begin{matrix}
( a_1 , A_1 ) & ( a_2 , A_2 ) & \ldots & ( a_p , A_p ) \\
( b_1 , B_1 ) & ( b_2 , B_2 ) & \ldots & ( b_q , B_q ) \end{matrix}
; z \right]
=
H^{1,p}_{p,q+1} \left[ -z \left| \begin{matrix}
( 1-a_1 , A_1 ) & ( 1-a_2 , A_2 ) & \ldots & ( 1-a_p , A_p ) \\
(0,1) & (1- b_1 , B_1 ) & ( 1-b_2 , B_2 ) & \ldots & ( 1-b_q , B_q ) \end{matrix} \right. \right].
</math>

== Wright function ==

The entire function <math>W_{\lambda,\mu}(z)</math> is often called '''the Wright function'''.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/WrightFunction.html |last=Weisstein |first=Eric W. |title=Wright Function |website=From MathWorld--A Wolfram Web Resource |access-date=2022-12-03}}</ref> It is the special case of <math>{}_0\Psi_1 \left[\ldots \right]</math> of the Fox–Wright function. Its series representation is

<math display="block">W_{\lambda,\mu}(z) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty
\frac{z^n}{n!\,\Gamma(\lambda n+\mu)}, \lambda > -1. </math>

This function is used extensively in [[fractional calculus]]. Recall that <math>\lim\limits_{\lambda \to 0} W_{\lambda,\mu}(z) = e^{z} / \Gamma(\mu)</math>. Hence, a non-zero <math>\lambda</math> with zero <math>\mu</math> is the simplest nontrivial extension of the [[exponential function]] in such context.

Three properties were stated in Theorem 1 of Wright (1933)<ref>{{cite journal |last=Wright |first=E. |date=1933 |title=On the Coefficients of Power Series Having Exponential Singularities |journal=Journal of the London Mathematical Society |series=Second Series |pages=71–79 |doi=10.1112/JLMS/S1-8.1.71 |s2cid=122652898 |language=en}}</ref> and 18.1(30–32) of Erdelyi, Bateman Project, Vol 3 (1955)<ref>{{Cite book |last=Erdelyi |first=A |title=The Bateman Project, Volume 3 |publisher=California Institute of Technology |year=1955}}</ref> (p. 212)

<math display="block">\begin{align}
\lambda z W_{\lambda,\mu+\lambda}(z) & = W_{\lambda,\mu -1}(z) + (1-\mu) W_{\lambda,\mu}(z)
& (a) \\[6pt]
{d \over dz} W_{\lambda,\mu }(z) & = W_{\lambda,\mu +\lambda}(z)
& (b) \\[6pt]
\lambda z {d \over dz} W_{\lambda,\mu }(z) & = W_{\lambda,\mu -1}(z) + (1-\mu) W_{\lambda,\mu}(z)
& (c)
\end{align}
</math>

Equation (a) is a recurrence formula. (b) and (c) provide two paths to reduce a derivative. And (c) can be derived from (a) and (b).

A special case of (c) is <math>\lambda = -c\alpha, \mu = 0</math>. Replacing <math>z</math> with <math>-x^\alpha</math>, we have

<math display="block">\begin{array}{lcl}
x {d \over dx} W_{-c\alpha,0 }(-x^\alpha) & = & 
  -\frac{1}{c} 
  \left[ W_{-c\alpha,-1}(-x^\alpha) + W_{-c\alpha,0}(-x^\alpha) \right]
\end{array}
</math>

A special case of (a) is <math>\lambda = -\alpha, \mu = 1</math>. Replacing <math>z</math> with <math>-z</math>, we have
<math display="block">\alpha z W_{-\alpha,1-\alpha}(-z) = W_{-\alpha,0}(-z)</math>

Two notations, <math>M_{\alpha}(z)</math> and <math>F_{\alpha}(z)</math>, were used extensively in the literatures:

<math display="block">\begin{align}
M_{\alpha}(z) & = W_{-\alpha,1-\alpha}(-z), \\ [1ex]
\implies
F_{\alpha}(z) & = W_{-\alpha,0}(-z) = \alpha z M_{\alpha}(z).
\end{align}
</math>

=== M-Wright function ===

<math>M_\alpha(z)</math> is known as the M-Wright function, entering as a probability density in a relevant class of self-similar stochastic processes, generally referred to as time-fractional diffusion processes.

Its properties were surveyed in Mainardi et al (2010).<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Mainardi |first1=Francesco |last2=Mura |first2=Antonio |last3=Pagnini |first3=Gianni |date=2010-02-11 |title=The M-Wright Function in Time-Fractional Diffusion Processes: A Tutorial Survey | journal=International Journal of Differential Equations |doi=10.1155/2010/104505 |volume=2010 |number=1 |article-number=104505 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

Its [[asymptotic expansion]] of <math>M_{\alpha}(z)</math> for <math>\alpha > 0</math> is
<math display="block">
M_\alpha \left ( \frac{r}{\alpha} \right ) =
A(\alpha) \, r^{(\alpha -1/2)/(1-\alpha)}
\, e^{-B(\alpha) \, r^{1/(1-\alpha)}}, \,\, r\rightarrow \infty,
</math>
where
<math> A(\alpha) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi (1-\alpha)}}, </math>
<math> B(\alpha) = \frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha}.</math>
